<explanation>
Based on our analysis of the file tree and README, this project is an open‐source Ruby library (gem) called factory_bot. It’s designed as a fixtures replacement tool by providing a DSL for defining object factories and supporting various build strategies (such as creating saved instances, unsaved instances, attribute hashes, and stubbed objects). The project also supports factory inheritance and integrates with testing tools like RSpec or tools in the Ruby ecosystem. With that in mind, here are detailed instructions to create a system design (architecture) diagram tailored for this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Client Code / Integration Layer – This represents the consumer of the gem (e.g., Rails, RSpec, or other Ruby applications that use factory_bot). It calls the public APIs to define and build object factories.
   • Public API / DSL Interface – Located primarily in lib/factory_bot and its syntax subdirectories (such as lib/factory_bot/syntax). This component exposes the DSL methods that clients use to define factories and traits.
   • Core Factory Engine – This includes modules for defining and managing factories (for example, lib/factory_bot/factory, lib/factory_bot/registry, lib/factory_bot/definition, and lib/factory_bot/definition_proxy). It holds the logic for registering, finding, and inheriting definitions.
   • Build Strategies & Evaluation – Group together the modules handling different strategies (found under lib/factory_bot/strategy with files like build.rb, create.rb, stub.rb, and attributes_for.rb). Also include evaluation and strategy selection elements (e.g., lib/factory_bot/evaluator, lib/factory_bot/strategy_calculator) that decide how an instance is built based on the chosen strategy.
   • Attribute and Sequence Handling – Components such as lib/factory_bot/attribute, lib/factory_bot/attribute/sequence, and lib/factory_bot/sequence are responsible for generating dynamic attributes and managing sequences.
   • Callbacks & Hooks – The modules that handle callback logic (like lib/factory_bot/callback and lib/factory_bot/callbacks_observer) ensure that lifecycle hooks are applied during object construction.
   • Error Handling, Linting, and Internal Utilities – This includes elements like lib/factory_bot/errors, lib/factory_bot/linter, and supporting modules that provide internal integrity checks.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   • Show a flow starting from the Client Code invoking the DSL methods from the Public API, which then delegates to the Core Factory Engine.
   • Indicate that the Core Engine registers factory definitions in the registry and uses the Attribute/Sequence components to generate attribute data.
   • Show that, upon building an instance, the engine selects a Build Strategy (for example, build vs. create vs. stub) which then triggers the Evaluation and Strategy Calculator components.
   • Represent that Callbacks or Hooks are invoked at key stages during the object-building lifecycle.
   • Label dependencies such as interaction between the DSL layer and configuration modules (e.g., lib/factory_bot/configuration) that might control behavior across the system.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Use of the Strategy Pattern for selecting among various build approaches.
   • Separation of concerns by dividing the DSL/API layer, factory definition/registration module, and build/evaluation components.
   • Emphasis on modularity and extensibility: Each of these modules (for attribute handling, sequence generation, associations, and callbacks) is kept separate.
   • Clear differentiation between the public interface (what the user directly interacts with) and internal mechanisms (factory registration, definition processing, evaluation).

4. Include Specific Technologies and Frameworks:
   • Ruby as the primary programming language and gem packaging.
   • Integration/invocation via testing frameworks such as RSpec (as seen in the spec/ directory) and usage with Rails (via the separate factory_bot_rails gem).
   • Continuous integration/workflow components hosted in .github/workflows (important for development but might not figure heavily into the runtime architecture diagram).

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Since this is an open-source library (not a full-stack application), focus on illustrating internal modules rather than separate infrastructure components like databases or network layers.
   • Emphasize the core modules (API/DSL, Factory Engine, Build Strategies, Attribute/Sequence, Callbacks) and show how they are orchestrated.
   • Use different colors or shapes to differentiate between public interfaces, internal processing modules, and testing/integration utilities.

6. Specific Diagram Elements for the Principal Software Engineer:
   • Create distinct nodes for:
       - "Client Code / Test Suites" (representing usage scenarios)
       - "Public DSL API" (exhibiting the entry points)
       - "Factory Definition & Registry" (the core module for managing factory definitions)
       - "Build Strategies" (with sub-nodes for create, build, stub, etc.)
       - "Attribute & Sequence Handlers"
       - "Callbacks & Hooks"
       - "Error/Linting & Utility Components"
   • Draw directional arrows to show the flow from client invocation through the API to the core engine and then into the strategy selection and evaluation processes.
   • Use labels on the arrows to denote key interactions (e.g., “invokes”, “registers”, “evaluates”, “applies callbacks”).
   • Optionally, use color coding or different shapes to help distinguish external integrations (e.g., client/test code) from internal processing modules.

7. Final Details:
   • Make the diagram detailed enough to capture every key architectural element but also organized so that the relationships (dependency and data flow) are clear.
   • Given that the project has a rich set of tests and documentation (reflected in both spec and docs directories), these assure us that modular boundaries have been well considered.
   • Stress that capturing these modules, patterns, and interactions in the diagram will provide both a high-level overview and a detailed view of how factory_bot functions as a library.

With these guidelines, the principal software engineer should be able to create a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately reflects the internal structure and interactions within factory_bot, tailored specifically to its role as an extensible open-source Ruby library for object factory generation.
</explanation>
